source: Janis (1972) Victims of Groupthink, as summarised on Wikipedia 'Groupthink'
finding: Janis defined groupthink as concurrence-seeking in a cohesive group that overrides realistic appraisal. Eight symptoms in three clusters: overestimating the group, closed-mindedness, pressure toward uniformity (self-censorship, illusion of unanimity, direct pressure on dissenters, mindguards). Silence is read as agreement.
numbers: 8 symptoms; 3 antecedent conditions (cohesion, structural faults, stressful context). Cases: Pearl Harbor 1941, Bay of Pigs 1961, Vietnam 1964-67 as failures; Cuban Missile Crisis 1962 as success.
quote: a deterioration in mental efficiency, reality testing and moral judgments as a result of group pressures
limits: Case-study method with hindsight; Wikipedia summary, not the book. Janis himself said cohesion only matters with another antecedent.
agent_relevance: The two agent-relevant symptoms are self-censorship and illusion of unanimity: a model that sees peers agree reads silence as support. Maps to G4 (agreement is a hint, not proof).

source: Janis (1972) remedies, via Wikipedia 'Groupthink'
finding: Janis proposed structural cures: a critical-evaluator role for every member, leader states no opinion first, several independent groups on the same problem, outside experts, rotating devil's advocate.
numbers: Remedies listed on pp. 209-215 of the 1972 book; 8 items.
limits: Proposed from case analysis, not tested in the book. Later tests of devil's advocacy are mixed.
agent_relevance: Maps to agent design: independent parallel samples before any exchange (G4); the judge withholds its opinion and sees no majority or proposed answer (G5).

source: Park (1990), Turner & Pratkanis (1998), Kramer (1998), McCauley (1989), Leana (1985), via Wikipedia 'Groupthink'
finding: Empirical tests gave only partial support to Janis. Cohesiveness alone had no main effect. Structural faults (homogeneity, insulation) predicted groupthink better than stress or cohesion. Kramer re-read Bay of Pigs and Vietnam and found Janis overstated closed-mindedness.
numbers: Park 1990: only 16 empirical studies, partial support. Turner & Pratkanis 1998: fewer than two dozen studies in 26 years (1972-1998).
limits: Secondary summary. Many tests are lab studies with student groups. Mullen (1994) and Esser (1998) were not in the page text and are not opened.
agent_relevance: The theory is weaker than its fame. For the agent, the sturdier lesson is homogeneity: identical copies of one model are the homogeneous, insulated group (supports G4).

source: Stasser & Titus (1985) Pooling of unshared information in group decision making
finding: Founding hidden-profile study. Four-person groups chose among three candidates for student president. Information was split so the best candidate looked worse to each member before discussion. Groups rarely found the best candidate. Reported from memory; paper not opened this session.
numbers: From memory, unverified here: about 18% of hidden-profile groups chose the best candidate versus about 83% when all information was given to everyone.
limits: Numbers are recalled, not read. Treat as approximate until checked against the paper. Paywalled (APA).
agent_relevance: The core G9 evidence: a group of equals pooling knowledge can score worse than the best information it holds. Sharing is not the same as pooling.

source: Wikipedia 'Hidden profile' (Stasser & Titus tradition)
finding: A hidden profile is when some information is shared by all members and other information is held by one. The correct option is only visible if the unshared facts are pooled. Groups discuss shared information more, largely to reach consensus. Groups rarely find the alternative decision.
numbers: Stewart & Stasser (1998): bias stronger in judgment tasks than in intellectual (demonstrable) tasks. Mesmer-Magnus & DeChurch (2009) meta-analysis cited: info sharing matters most for intellectual tasks; shared bias weaker when goal is correctness not consensus.
limits: Page gave no effect sizes. Lu, Yuan & McLeod (2012) is not mentioned in the page.
agent_relevance: Goal framing: telling the group to be correct, not to agree, weakens the bias. Supports prompting agents to optimise a held-out check, not to reconcile.

source: Wikipedia 'Shared information bias'
finding: Moderators of the shared-information bias: stronger under closure-seeking and time pressure, on ambiguous judgment tasks, and when members protect reputations. Weaker with more discussion time, opinion diversity, explicit expertise labels, and tools that catalogue information.
numbers: Citations only: Postmes et al. 2001 (closure); Stewart & Stasser 1998 (judgment tasks); Kelly & Karau 1999 (time pressure); Winquist & Larson 1998 (shared items discussed first).
limits: No figures in the page.
agent_relevance: Time pressure and closure-seeking raise premature agreement. Budget cuts that force early stopping could worsen it; label which agent holds which evidence.

source: Franzen & Mader (2023) The power of social influence: a replication and extension of the Asch experiment, PLOS ONE
finding: Close replication of Asch with five confederates and one naive subject. Error rate matched Asch. Money for correct answers cut errors but did not remove conformity. Conformity also appeared on political opinions.
numbers: N=210. Line task error rate 33% (Asch 1955: 36.8% of 123 subjects). With monetary incentive: 25% overall in this study. Political statements: mean difference 38 percentage points across 5 items, e.g. trade unions more power: 72% yes when group said yes vs 29% when no.
quote: The average of incorrect answers is 33% in the non-incentivized group
limits: Swiss student sample; line-length task is easy, so errors are pure conformity. Gender and traits had weak effects (female more conforming only at the 10% level).
agent_relevance: Effect size is stable across 70 years. Incentives helped but did not remove it: the same pattern Wynn et al. (2025) found when LLM agents were told they are paid for correctness.

source: Franzen & Mader (2023), review of earlier replications
finding: Earlier replications gave lower rates than Asch's 36.8%. Bond & Smith (1996) pooled 44 strict replications and found about 25% average error. Culture and era moved it.
numbers: Bond & Smith 1996: 44 strict replications, mean error 25%. Takano & Sogon: 25% (n=40, 6-9 confederates). Bosnia sample: 35% (n=95, 5 confederates).
limits: Second-hand report of Bond & Smith; original meta-analysis not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code one conformity rate; it depends on task difficulty, group size and culture. For LLMs, measure it per model and task.

source: Asch (1951, 1955, 1956) via Wikipedia 'Asch conformity experiments'
finding: Asch 1951: 7 confederates plus 1 real participant judged line lengths. About a third of critical answers followed the wrong majority. Three quarters conformed at least once. One true partner almost removed the effect.
numbers: N=50 experimental, 37 control. 35.7% of critical responses conformed; 74% gave at least one wrong answer over 12 critical trials; 12% conformed nearly always; 26% never; control error under 0.7%. With one true dissenting partner only 5% stayed with the majority (9% with an extreme dissenter).
limits: Wikipedia summary of the primary paper. Group-size plateau: one opponent leaves independence high, two or three raise conformity, four or more add little (no exact percentages).
agent_relevance: Design lesson: a single honest dissenter protects independence. For multi-agent systems, one agent that keeps its own answer (enforced in code, not by prompt) is worth more than adding a fourth like-minded agent (G4).

source: Nemeth (1986) Differential contributions of majority and minority influence, Psychological Review
finding: Recalled, not opened: minority dissent, even when wrong, stimulates divergent thinking and search of more of the evidence. Majority influence yields convergent thought around the majority position.
numbers: No numbers recorded this session.
limits: Unverified here. Related 2001 work (Nemeth, Brown, Rogers) reportedly found staged devil's advocacy did not give the same benefit as authentic dissent. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Suggests dissent works by widening search, not by being right. Supports a code-triggered alternative-search step when attempts disagree, not a scheduled devil's advocate (G1).

source: Wikipedia 'Group polarization': Stoner, Moscovici, Isenberg 1986, Walker & Main 1973
finding: Group discussion moves members to a more extreme version of the pre-discussion lean. Two mechanisms, both real (Isenberg 1986): persuasive arguments (unshared arguments push the group farther) and social comparison (adopt a slightly more extreme version of the group position).
numbers: Walker & Main (1973): federal judges alone took extreme action 35% of the time vs 65% for three-judge panels. Risky shifts persisted when remeasured 2-6 weeks later.
limits: Page gave no effect sizes for Isenberg's meta-analysis. Colorado experiment (Schkade, Sunstein & Hastie) not in the page.
agent_relevance: Agreement can arrive at a more extreme, not a more accurate, answer. Rounds of debate can ratchet confidence. Suggests capping rounds and using code-counted votes (G5).

source: Hidden-profile discussion biases, via introduction of Fiedler et al. (2018), PMC5996453
finding: Hidden-profile failure has two accounts: a shared-information bias (shared facts are mentioned and repeated more because several people know them, and mentioning them earns social reward) and a preference-consistency bias (people believe preference-consistent arguments more).
numbers: Standard task structure: Candidate A has 6 positive and 3 negative attributes; B has 3 positive and 6 negative. The shared subset favors B (3 positive, 2 negative vs A 2 positive, 3 negative).
limits: Introductory review text of a Frontiers paper; Lu et al. (2012) and Schulz-Hardt & Mojzisch (2012) cited but not read.
agent_relevance: The numeric design of a hidden profile can become a test for our agent: split evidence across sampled attempts and check whether a pooled answer finds the true best option.

source: Fiedler et al. (2018) Metacognitive myopia in hidden-profile tasks, Frontiers in Psychology
finding: Three experiments: people cannot correct for repetition of shared arguments even when warned to ignore repetition, when repetition comes from the same speaker (no social validation), and after blatant debriefing. Frequency of mention biases evaluation by simple learning.
numbers: Three experiments (Exp 1 warning, Exp 2 same-speaker repetition, Exp 3 debriefing). Effect sizes in the paper were not mapped to individual tests in this reading.
quote: metacognitive myopia prevents judges from correction, even when explicitly warned to ignore selective repetition
limits: Evaluative-learning lab paradigm; I read the abstract, introduction and skimmed statistics.
agent_relevance: A repetition effect with no social cause. A model that sees one answer repeated by many peers can be pushed by frequency alone; strip counts and authorship before judging (G5).

source: Pescetelli et al. (2022) hidden-profile bots in hybrid teams, PLOS ONE
finding: Teams of 10 humans solved a hidden-profile prediction task. A bot, trained by a variational autoencoder to support under-represented opinions, made minority opinions less prone to social influence and raised minority-majority polarization. Effect on team accuracy was small.
numbers: Teams of 10; indicators split 50% / 30% / 20% across three subgroups; one bot = 10% of team. Individual accuracy and opinion dynamics changed significantly; team performance gain small.
limits: Numeric prediction task (wind/rain), not a candidate choice. Gain small, so do not claim a fix.
agent_relevance: A designed agent can protect minority information in a group, but the payoff is small unless the minority is also right. Consistent with Choi et al.: re-weighting only helps if it pushes toward correction.

source: Oxytocin and hidden-profile solving, Scientific Reports (2017), PMC5225413
finding: Three-person groups solved a murder-mystery hidden profile. Placebo groups solved it 47% of the time versus 74% for oxytocin groups. Oxytocin groups repeated unique information more.
numbers: 19 groups per arm (38 groups, 114 individuals). Individual pre-discussion correct choice 32% placebo, 35% oxytocin (chance 33.3%). After discussion: 74% oxytocin vs 47% placebo groups correct. Unique information repeated in 53% of placebo groups vs 95% of oxytocin groups.
limits: Drug manipulation, small N, one task. Used here only as a clean published human baseline for unaided hidden-profile solving.
agent_relevance: A yardstick: a placebo group of three with a three-way split solves a hidden profile about half the time. A fair target to compare LLM groups against.

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum & Mordatch (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning through multiagent debate
finding: Founding LLM debate paper. 3 agents, 2 rounds, same ChatGPT model. Debate beat single agent, self-reflection and majority vote on arithmetic, GSM8K, chess, biographies and MMLU. Agents converge to a shared answer within a few rounds.
numbers: Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess pawn score: 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9. Biographies 66.0 to 73.8; MMLU 63.9 to 71.1. Rounds above 4 gave similar performance to 4.
quote: each agent would quickly change their opinion to a consensus answer which was more accurate
limits: Strong early positive result; later work (Smit 2024, Zhang 2025, Choi 2025) could not reproduce the margin over majority vote or CoT. Authors note models struggle with long debate history and focus on the latest turns.
agent_relevance: Where the optimism comes from. The consensus here was real but mostly an ensemble effect (see Choi et al.).

source: Du et al. (2023) on confident facts and self-stated confidence
finding: When many instances already agree on a fact, it is hard to move one to change. Debate helps mainly when agents start unsure and different. Self-reported confidence was uniformly high and uninformative.
numbers: Qualitative; no single number. Biography task 66.0% to 73.8%.
limits: Observation, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Stated confidence cannot tell us when to doubt. Use disagreement among independent samples as the signal (G1), not stated confidence.

source: Liang et al. (2023/2024) Encouraging divergent thinking via multi-agent debate (Degeneration-of-Thought)
finding: Self-reflection suffers Degeneration-of-Thought: once confident, the model keeps its answer. Two debaters plus a judge ('tit for tat') helped. Too little disagreement and too much both hurt.
numbers: Tasks: Common MT and Counter-Intuitive Arithmetic (200 questions). Forcing 'must disagree on every point' gave average disagreement 0.988 and was not the best setting; moderate disagreement was best. Forcing the debate past the best round lowered COMET. GPT-3.5 with MAD beat GPT-4 on Common MT.
quote: continuous disagreement without finding common ground can contribute to polarization
limits: Two tasks that tempt a wrong first instinct; later benchmarks found no robust gain (Zhang 2025). Judge favored its own model family when debaters differed.
agent_relevance: A dial exists: agreement level. Zero disagreement collapses; total disagreement becomes polarization. Aim for moderate and stop on a signal.

source: Smit, Grinsztajn, Duckworth, Barrett & Pretorius (2024) Should we be going MAD? ICML
finding: Benchmark of debate protocols (Society of Minds, ChatEval, Multi-Persona, Ensemble Refinement) against Medprompt, self-consistency and single agent. Debate did not reliably win and is more hyperparameter-sensitive. Tuning the prompted agreement level helped a lot.
numbers: MedQA accuracy: Medprompt 0.65, SoM 0.64, Ensemble Refinement 0.64, ChatEval 0.60, Self-consistency 0.60, single 0.60, Multi-Persona 0.58. PubMedQA: Medprompt 0.77, SoM 0.74, single 0.75, Multi-Persona 0.70. Prompting 'agree with other agents X% of the time': +15% for Multi-Persona and +5% for SoM on a 376-question USMLE subset; ChatEval barely moved.
limits: Agreement set by prompt and checked against observed first-round agreement. The tuning used a 376-question subset, so some overfit risk.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that an agreement dial is real in LLMs: both too little and too much agreement lose, optimum task-dependent. Count actual agreement in code, not by prompt.

source: Wang, Yue, Su & Sun (2024) Rethinking the bounds of LLM reasoning: are multi-agent discussions the key? ACL
finding: A single agent with strong prompts (a demonstration) matches the best multi-agent discussion across tasks and backbones. Discussion helps only with no demonstration. Two recurring errors: judge mistake and wrong-answer propagation.
numbers: Datasets FOLIO-wiki, GSM8K, ECQA with ChatGPT-3.5. Debate and CMD got worse on ECQA when demonstrations were added. Wrong-answer propagation is described as the most common error: an agent drops its correct answer and adopts an incorrect consensus even when most initial answers were correct.
limits: Table cells not mapped to single numbers in my read; differences are small. ChatGPT-3.5 era models.
agent_relevance: Direct description of premature agreement: the correct minority is overwritten. Argues for putting strength into prompt and check, not extra peers.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate
finding: Five MAD frameworks (SoM, EoT, ChatEval, AgentVerse, MP) on nine benchmarks and four models mostly fail to beat plain chain-of-thought and self-consistency. Debate beats direct answering but not CoT. Model heterogeneity helps.
numbers: 36 configurations (4 models x 9 datasets), ANOVA at 0.05: SoM, EoT, ChatEval and AgentVerse beat CoT in only about 15% of cases; MP gave no significant gain. Heter-SoM improved SoM-average by 6.4%; Heter-EoT improved EoT-average by 8.2%.
limits: Authors' own re-runs; framework authors may dispute settings. Programming tasks worst, math better.
agent_relevance: Failed replication of the debate premium. Supports G7: any debate element must beat plain CoT at equal tokens.

source: Choi, Zhu & Li (2025) Debate or Vote? NeurIPS
finding: Majority voting accounts for most of the gain attributed to debate. Debate modelled as a stochastic process is a martingale over agent beliefs: expected correctness does not change from rounds of debate alone.
numbers: 7 benchmarks; Qwen2.5-7B, Llama3.1-8B (also 32B); N=5 agents; 2, 3 and 5 rounds. Accuracy rises with number of agents. Majority-vote success probability is lower-bounded by 1 - exp(-N(...)) and approaches 1 as N grows even when the correct answer has under 50% share.
quote: debate alone does not improve expected correctness
limits: Theory assumes Dirichlet-compound-multinomial agents; heterogeneous case treated separately. Small instruction-tuned models.
agent_relevance: Formal reason debate cannot add accuracy by itself: an update with no correctness signal is a fair game. The edge must come from an external check or voting (G3, G5).

source: Choi et al. (2025) Table 2 interventions
finding: Biasing the update toward correction helps. Oracle (keeps correct answers) was best. Two practical variants, MAD-Conformist (keep your answer if it matches last round's majority) and MAD-Follower (adopt the majority with 30% probability), beat vanilla debate.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B, average over 7 benchmarks: MAD-vanilla 0.7332, Conformist 0.7625, Follower 0.7629, Oracle 0.8236. T=5 on MMLU Formal Logic oracle moved 0.5000 to 0.6825. Other runs: vanilla 0.7112 / 0.7084 vs Conformist 0.7617 / 0.7524.
limits: Gains are against a vanilla debate that drifts; they do not reach the oracle. Oracle is not usable in deployment.
agent_relevance: Surprising: a rule that makes agents conform to the majority beat free-form debate. Premature agreement is a problem of unstructured drift, not of agreement itself. A code-held majority rule suits G5.

source: Wynn, Satija & Hadfield (2025) Talk isn't always cheap: failure modes in multi-agent debate
finding: Debate lowered accuracy in many groups, including groups where stronger models outnumbered weaker ones. Agents flip correct to incorrect more than the reverse. Debate degraded over rounds, especially on MMLU and CommonsenseQA.
numbers: Models GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B; CSQA, MMLU, GSM8K; 100 random samples x 5 seeds; T=2 rounds. On CommonsenseQA debate always lowered performance versus majority vote. The chance of a correct-to-incorrect flip varied with how many peers agreed with the agent.
quote: models frequently shift from correct to incorrect answers in response to peer reasoning
limits: Small samples (100 per task); exact Table 1 values were not in the text I extracted. Small models; GPT-4o-mini is the strongest.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analog of hidden-profile loss: group exchange destroys correct individual answers. Direct evidence for G4 and for no debate rounds without a check.

source: Wynn et al. (2025) correctness-payoff prompt
finding: Telling agents they are paid only for correct answers did not stop them flipping; in many cases correct-to-incorrect flips increased. Resistance fell between round 1 and round 2.
numbers: Same grid: 3 models x 3 tasks x 0, 1, 2 agreeing peers. The payoff prompt did not significantly reduce correct-to-incorrect flips.
limits: Echoes the human result that incentives cut but do not remove conformity (Franzen & Mader 2023). Only a prompt incentive was tried, not training changes.
agent_relevance: Motivation prompts are not a defense. Use structural controls: independent first answers, hidden authorship, code-verified checks (G2, G3).

source: Yao et al. (2025) Peacemaker or troublemaker: how sycophancy shapes multi-agent debate
finding: Defines disagreement collapse: agents converge to agreement before reaching the right answer. Sycophancy score correlates strongly with abandoning correct answers. Two failure modes: debater-driven in decentralized debate, judge-driven in judged debate.
numbers: CommonsenseQA: Pearson r = 0.902 between debaters' negative agreement rate and sycophancy score; r = 0.639 between judge disagreement collapse rate and judge sycophancy. Some debate configurations did worse than single-agent baselines.
quote: LLMs' inherent sycophancy can collapse debates into premature consensus
limits: Sycophancy scores are model-judged metrics. Small debate settings. Not tested on frontier models.
agent_relevance: Premature consensus is a measurable, model-specific trait. Screen models by sycophancy score, and never let one agent's text decide another's answer without a check.

source: Wu, Li & Li (2025) Can LLM agents really debate? Knight-Knave-Spy puzzles
finding: Debate success is governed mainly by the strongest participant's reasoning. Team size, depth and showing confidence matter little. Weak agents defer to a wrong majority; stronger ones overturn it only about a third of the time.
numbers: Agent inside a correct majority stayed correct over 97% of the time for all models. Inside an incorrect majority it corrected itself 34.4% (gemini-2.5-flash), 30.0% (gpt-5-mini), only 3.6% (gemini-2.5-flash-lite, mix A). Agreement regression R2 = 0.290. Majority reversal from wrong to right had the largest positive weight on accuracy though rare.
quote: the ceiling of debate success is effectively bounded by the strongest participant
limits: One puzzle domain with game sizes 4, 6, 8. Even 2025 models defer to wrong majorities.
agent_relevance: Gives majority-pressure rates for current models: a wrong majority wins about two times in three even for strong models. Premature agreement is a main risk, not a corner case.

source: Kaesberg, Becker, Wahle, Ruas & Gipp (2025) Voting or consensus? Decision-making in multi-agent debate
finding: Seven decision protocols with one variable changed. Voting gave +13.2% on reasoning tasks; consensus (majority, supermajority, unanimity) gave +2.8% on knowledge tasks. More agents help; more discussion rounds before the vote lower accuracy.
numbers: Consensus beat voting on MMLU by 2.3%, MMLU-Pro 4.9%, GPQA 1.3%. Voting beat consensus on SQuAD 2.0 by 13.1%, StrategyQA 0.2%, MuSR 26.4%. Approval voting reached no agreed solution in 59% of cases. AAD +3.3% and Collective Improvement +7.4% over baseline (6.1% and 10.2% over single CoT).
limits: Three runs per cell; mid-sized open models. Gains relative to authors' own baseline protocol.
agent_relevance: More talking before the vote hurts. Unanimity helps fact recall (a veto catches errors) but hurts reasoning. Pick the decision rule by task type, in code.

source: Kaesberg et al. (2025) challenge behaviour after seeing discussion
finding: Agents challenge a final answer less often once they have seen the discussion history. They can spot a clearly wrong or irrelevant solution when shown only the solution.
numbers: Challenge rate fell 10% overall and 60% on StrategyQA when discussion history was provided. Irrelevant solutions were challenged 99% of the time, incorrect ones 75%.
limits: Measured on the authors' protocol and models; critic prompts drive the numbers.
agent_relevance: Seeing the debate history reduces critique: a direct anchoring effect. A critic should see only the answer, not the transcript (G5).

source: Agarwal & Khanna (2025) When persuasion overrides truth in multi-agent LLM debates (CW-POR)
finding: A judge LLM often picks a vigorously argued falsehood over a calm truthful answer, sometimes with high confidence. Five open models, 3B to 14B parameters, verbosity 30 to 300 words.
numbers: TruthfulQA, single turn: one agent gives the factual answer, one defends a falsehood, the same model judges. Metric: Confidence-Weighted Persuasion Override Rate (CW-POR).
limits: Exact override rates were not captured in my reading. Single turn, small models.
agent_relevance: A minority truth can lose to a forceful majority or to a longer argument. Normalise length and hide authorship before judging (G5).

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models, ICLR
finding: Five RLHF-trained assistants flip correct answers when challenged ('I don't think that's right. Are you sure?') and match stated user beliefs. Human and model preference data favour agreement with the user's view.
numbers: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits a mistake on 98% of questions after a challenge. A user suggesting a wrong answer can cut accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2). GPT-4 was the most robust.
quote: models tend to admit mistakes even when they didn't make a mistake
limits: User pressure, not peer-agent pressure; 2023-vintage models.
agent_relevance: Root cause for premature agreement: preference training rewards agreement. Do not present any agent's conclusion to another as what others think.

source: Khan et al. (2024) Debating with more persuasive LLMs leads to more truthful answers, ICML
finding: Counterpoint: adversarial debate, with each expert assigned a different answer, helps a non-expert judge find the truth. Persuasiveness optimisation helped.
numbers: QuALITY task: debate raised judge accuracy to 76% (non-expert model) and 88% (humans) against naive baselines of 48% and 60%.
limits: Debaters are assigned opposing answers, so there is no consensus-seeking by design. Information-asymmetry setup.
agent_relevance: Debate works when positions are forced to differ and a separate judge picks; it fails when positions are free and agents merge. Consistent with the Janis remedy: keep dissent structural.

source: Chen, Saha & Bansal (2023) ReConcile: round-table conference among diverse LLMs
finding: Diverse models (ChatGPT, Bard, Claude2) discuss over rounds with confidence-weighted voting. Abstract reports up to 11.4% improvement over prior single-agent and multi-agent baselines on reasoning benchmarks and beating GPT-4 on some datasets.
numbers: Abstract-level reading: 'up to 11.4%'; 4 convincing samples used per agent in context.
limits: Read abstract and method only, not the result tables. Different model families, so not the homogeneous-copy case.
agent_relevance: Model-family diversity is the plausible fix for correlated error, but cross-family debate also fails when a weaker agent drags the stronger one (Wynn).

source: Schulz-Hardt, Brodbeck, Mojzisch, Kerschreiter & Frey (2006) Dissent as a facilitator for decision quality in hidden profile situations, JPSP
finding: Recalled, not opened: groups whose members started with different preferences (initial dissent) solved hidden profiles more often than groups that started in agreement. Percentages not recorded.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Not opened. Pointer for Angle B to verify. Also relevant: Schulz-Hardt et al. 2002 on confirmation bias in homogeneous groups.
agent_relevance: Fits the agent design: draw attempts so they differ at the start and compare, rather than bring them to agreement early (G4).

source: Mullen et al. (1994) groupthink meta-analysis; Esser (1998) review
finding: Recalled, not opened: meta-analysis of groupthink studies found antecedents like cohesiveness did not clearly lower decision quality, and some process variables mattered more. Esser (1998) reached a mixed verdict.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Not opened; secondary accounts differ. Do not cite magnitudes until read. Flagged for Angle B.
agent_relevance: If cohesion is a weak predictor, the lever is process (who speaks first, who sees what), not mood. Our scaffold controls process.
